properties.decision:
**RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.** Anthony, 2026-08-26, in his own words:

*"can we construct skills or tools in a factory that ensures they get the required mechanics/functions? then when we need to make a 'class' change, it is fixing the factory, not the individual skill."*

📌 DISTINCT FROM `dec:idea-a-tool-class-should-carry-a-contract-that-something-checks`, which asks WHAT a class must guarantee. This asks HOW the guarantee is delivered — by construction, or by inspection after the fact. Both answers are available for any contract, and the choice between them is the whole content here.

═══ THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS ═══

**A CHECK finds the omission after somebody made it. A FACTORY makes the omission unconstructable.** Today's fix is the first: `every_category_states_whether_it_reads_proposed` catches an unclassified category at compile time, but only after somebody wrote it. A factory would mean a finding kind cannot come into existence without answering.

This is the shape Anthony is reaching for, and the payoff he names is real: **a class change becomes one edit instead of N.** Today's change edited three call sites for one rule. The three instances this week each edited between one and three sites. Nothing has yet needed editing across all 173 tools — which is either evidence the problem is small, or evidence it has not bitten yet.

═══ WHAT ALREADY EXISTS, because the answer is not "nothing" ═══

- **`#[tool]` is already a proc macro** — construction already runs through a single point. Whether it can be made to REQUIRE annotations is a technical question nobody has asked. This is the most promising unexamined lead here.
- **`skill_lint.py`, 1126 lines** — the inspection route, already built and already large.
- **`HealCategory::ALL` plus two exhaustive-match tests** — the compile-time route at its smallest, and it works.
- **The 12 tool-surface slices** — a classification that already exists and deliberately holds no function.

═══ OPTIONS, none chosen ═══

**(a) EXTEND THE `#[tool]` MACRO to require the annotation set.** The factory Anthony describes, in the place construction already happens. Missing annotation = compile error, no list to maintain. ⚠️ Counter: proc-macro work is unpleasant to debug, and a required field with a default is not required at all — the design would have to refuse silence, which means touching all 173 declarations once.

**(b) A CONSTRUCTOR FUNCTION / TRAIT rather than a macro change.** Each tool built through a typed builder that cannot be finished incomplete. ⚠️ Counter: heavier than the macro that is already there, and the macro is the thing standing between the author and the surface.

**(c) KEEP INSPECTION, MAKE IT EXHAUSTIVE.** No factory; just ensure every class has one test asserting every member answers. ⚠️ Counter: this is what the repo already does, and it is what let three instances through — each guard was written after its own incident, never before the next.

**(d) NOT WORTH IT YET.** No class change has ever required editing more than three sites. ⚠️ Counter: the cost being counted is wrong — the expensive part was never the editing, it was the DISCOVERY, and each discovery came from a user hitting it in the field.

═══ ⚠️ THE COUNTERWEIGHTS, and there are two real ones ═══

**1. A factory guarantees the mechanics are PRESENT, never that they are RIGHT.** Every instance this week was a case where the mechanism existed and the JUDGEMENT was missing — `unallocated_component` could have read the ruling, the replay contract was written down, `proposed` was documented in four places. A factory that injects a required field produces 173 tools with a field filled in to satisfy the compiler. That is the `internal`-by-default trap the interface `designation` field already documents: *"BECAUSE it is the default, `internal` cannot distinguish 'deliberately internal' from 'nobody classified this'."* **A factory can manufacture exactly that ambiguity at scale.**

**2. Over-engineering, and it is his own standing concern.** *"designs get so overcomplicated when often a simple solution will do."* A factory, a registry and a class taxonomy is the shape an engineer reaches for. The measured alternative is one exhaustive match per class — roughly fifteen lines, no new machinery, and it has now worked twice in the same file.

⇒ Which suggests the cheapest honest test: **name a change that WOULD have required editing all 173 tools.** If one exists, the factory earns itself. If none does, option (d) is the answer and the exhaustive-match habit is enough.
properties.name: DECIDED — skills are COMPOSED of attribute classes, not stamped by one factory and not swept by one exhaustive check
properties.rationale:
SETTLED BY ANTHONY, 2026-08-28, on option (f) — an option the original (a)–(d) did not contain, because they all assumed ONE factory stamping every member of a class identically.

HIS FRAMING: *"I didn't mean we have only one factory... like in python, a class can inherit a class which can inherit a class (I actually prefer class composition versus class inheritance). so a particular class of skills inherits a set of classes that determine what that skill should have."* And: *"I prefer building skills with composable blocks (and potentially using dependency injection if that can be done in rust). I also feel like it fits the MOSA type concept better than exhaustive checks."*

═══ WHAT SETTLED THE TWO COUNTERWEIGHTS ═══

**COUNTERWEIGHT 1 IS DISSOLVED, NOT OVERRULED.** *"A factory guarantees the mechanics are PRESENT, never that they are RIGHT."* True of a single factory, which must demand a section from all 23 and would get filler from the 15 that do not need it. COMPOSITION DEMANDS IT ONLY OF THE CLASS THAT OWES IT — "honest limits" from the skills that MEASURE, where its absence is a real omission. **The manufactured-ambiguity trap comes from UNIFORMITY, not from construction.**

**COUNTERWEIGHT 2 — OVER-ENGINEERING — WAS ANSWERED BY MEASUREMENT, AND THE MEASURED ALTERNATIVE FAILED.** This node's own recommendation was that one exhaustive match per class is enough. CHECKED AGAINST SOURCE 2026-08-28: the exhaustive check was BUILT and IS RUNNING over every skill — `served_skills.rs` iterates `SKILLS` three times, `skill_lint` walks every directory. And every one of its assertions is a UNIVERSAL predicate. A flat loop over a flat set cannot express "this skill owes REPORTS mechanics and that one does not". It did not fail; it succeeded at its scope, which is why the one universal mechanic is at 23/23 and every other is at 5–18. **"Just add an exhaustive check" was tried and is structurally unable to reach the case.** See `fact:the-exhaustive-check-was-built-and-can-only-carry-universal-obligations`.

═══ THE NODE'S OWN TEST, ANSWERED ═══

It posed: *"name a change that WOULD have required editing all 173 tools."* Unanswered for tools; answered for skills. "Speak the reader's domain" is §35 of the SERVED INSTRUCTIONS, stated as applying to every skill — carried in ONE of 23 skill bodies, enforced by ONE of three hand-written contracts, added only after two users independently invented the same workaround. A universal rule, implemented once, discovered late.

═══ ⭐ AND A SECOND REASON, WHICH IS ANTHONY'S AND IS NOT SUPERFICIAL ═══

*"having reflow2 reflect all the principles it says it will do for other projects is not necessarily a functional win, but it is a 'marketing' win in terms that reflow2 'looks the part'... little details like these make a difference."*

It is stronger than he states it. `dec:mosa-conformance` asks whether reflow2 should REPORT MOSA CONFORMANCE for other people's designs, given it already computes most of the criteria. **Its own skill surface would fail the severability criterion** — three contracts that cannot be composed, applied selectively, or replaced independently. That is not presentation; it is the tool exhibiting the property it flags. And it sits with the dogfooding rationale already on `chg:user-is-still-the-reminder`: using the thing is the instrument that finds its defects.

⚠️ THIS IS NOT A BREACH OF `rule:reflow2-is-built-for-other-projects-not-for-itself`. That rule forbids building FEATURES for reflow2's own sake. This applies reflow2's OWN STATED PRINCIPLES to its own construction, which is the rule's premise rather than an exception to it.

═══ 🛑 WHAT IS STILL UNCHOSEN, AND IT IS NOT SMALL ═══

**WHERE THE COMPOSITION LIVES.** Three candidates with materially different costs, none priced: (i) `skill_lint.py` — cheapest, Python, refactors the three existing contracts into composable sets, blocks in CI; (ii) a `composes:` list in each SKILL.md's frontmatter that the lint reads — makes the obligation legible to the AGENT reading the skill, not only to CI; (iii) the Rust build, strongest and most expensive. **Rust has no inheritance at all, so composition via traits is the only idiom available there — and the codebase already does constructor injection at `KvBackend` (a six-method trait, two implementations, `Box<dyn KvBackend>` in `StorageEngine`).**

**AND THE CLASS CARVING IS UNTESTED.** STANDING / WRITES / REVISES / REPORTS / MEASURES / DESTROYS is one agent's reading of 23 skills. A skill landing in four of them is a sign the carving is wrong, and nobody has tried it against the real set.
